etymologies.etymologyHTML: From dis- +‎ card. Compare Spanish descartar.

quote.citation: 1832, [Isaac Taylor], Saturday Evening. […], London: Holdsworth and Ball, →OCLC:
quote.text: A man discards the follies of boyhood.

quote.citation: 2020 December 2, Paul Bigland, “My weirdest and wackiest Rover yet”, in Rail, pages 67–68:
quote.text: My next stop is Oxford, which has also grown with the addition of new platforms to accommodate the Chiltern Railways service to London via Bicester - although, short sightedly, the planned electrification from Paddington was canned. Evidence of the volte-face can be seen along the line at places such as Radley, where mast piles are already sunk or lie discarded at the lineside.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, card games) To make a discard; to throw out a card.
To dismiss from employment, confidence, or favour; to discharge.

quote.citation: 1711 December 8 (Gregorian calendar), [Jonathan Swift], The Conduct of the Allies, and of the Late Ministry, in Beginning and Carrying on the Present War, 4th edition, London:  […]  John Morphew […], published 1711, →OCLC, page 65:
quote.text: […]  They blame the Favourites in point of Policy, and think it nothing extraordinary, that the Queen ſhould be at an end of Her Patience, and reſolve to diſcard them.

definitions.definition: A discarded playing card in a card game.
(programming) A temporary variable used to receive a value of no importance and unable to be read later.

quote.citation: 2017, Andrew Troelsen, Philip Japikse, Pro C# 7: With .NET and .NET Core, page 120:
quote.text: Discards can be used with out parameters, with tuples, with pattern matching (Chapters 6 and 8), or even as stand-alone variables.
